name: Blackish Slate
lede: Blackish Slate is a near-black shade of [[slate|slate]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body:
Blackish Slate pairs the modifier *blackish* with the base color [[slate]], Ridgway's plain naming grammar for a darker, less saturated member of a color family [1][4]. His 1912 *Color Standards and Nomenclature* gives it plate LIII, hue 75, close to neutral on his notation (Munsell-style N 3.1), with almost no measurable chroma [1]. The same pairing is not new to that plate: Ridgway had already used 'blackish slate' in his earlier 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, twenty-six years before [1].

The ISCC-NBS system filed the same block, 266, under the plain-language name 'dark grayish green,' close to Ridgway's hue at a Delta-E of 3.0 [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dusky-purplish-grey]] and [[blackish-plumbeous]], at 2.9 and 3.7 ΔE [1][4]. The color graph also cross-references a near Japanese shade, Onando-iro (御納戸色), literally 'storage-room color,' a name for a traditional grey once used for storeroom furnishings; it is a translation match on hue, not a claim that the two naming systems share a history [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 2.27% of 23,781 paintings, 540 paintings; within a single painting it reads as a distinct area in 259 of them [3]. That makes it more common than 75% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, found in 3.2% of that century's 1,674 paintings, 2.7 times the expected rate against the same museums' baseline [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, by lightness rank within the canvas, in 30% of its 259 appearances, a role varnish and photography cannot fake [3]. Paul Cezanne uses it most, in 8 of his 50 works in our archive, 7.4 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. Its earliest dated appearance is a painting from 1099, 787 years before the name's first documented record in 1886 [3]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first, and the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any pigment or dye [3]. It shares canvases with [[pale-umber]] more often than chance, a lift of 2.4 [3].
